content.text: The contributions of this paper are threefold. 1) We introduce the dynamic span graph frame- work as a method to propagate global contextual information, making the code publicly available. 2) We demonstrate that our framework signiﬁcantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on joint entity and relation detection tasks across four datasets: ACE 2004, ACE 2005, SciERC and the Wet Lab Proto- col Corpus. 3) We further show that our approach excels at detecting entities with overlapping spans, achieving an improvement of up to 8 F1 points on three benchmarks annotated with overlapped spans: ACE 2004, ACE 2005 and GENIA.

We evaluate D Y GIE on several datasets span- ning many domains (including news, scientiﬁc arti- cles, and wet lab experimental protocols), achiev- ing state-of-the-art performance across all tasks and domains and demonstrating the value of coupling related tasks to learn richer span representations. For example, D Y GIE achieves relative improve- ments of  $5.7\%$   and  $9.9\%$   over state of the art on the ACE05 entity and relation extraction tasks, and an  $11.3\%$   relative improvement on the ACE05 over- lapping entity extraction task.

The  ACE2004  and  ACE2005  corpora provide entity and relation labels for a collection of docu- ments from a variety of domains, such as newswire and online forums. content.text: The  SciERC  corpus ( Luan et al. ,  2018a ) pro- vides entity, coreference and relation annotations for a collection of documents from 500 AI paper abstracts. The dataset deﬁnes scientiﬁc term types and relation types specially designed for AI domain knowledge graph construction. An entity predic- tion is considered correct if its label and span match with a gold entity.

For the entity and relation extraction task, we test the performance of D Y GIE on four different datasets: ACE2004, ACE2005, SciERC and the Wet Lab Protocol Corpus. We include the rela- tion graph propagation layer in our models for all datasets. We include the coreference graph propa- gation layer on the data sets that have coreference annotations available.

The  GENIA  corpus ( Kim et al. ,  2003 ) provides entity tags and coreferences for 1999 abstracts from the biomedical research literature. We only use the IDENT label to extract coreference clusters.

Up gradation  of  Wafer  Fabrication  Lab  has  been  completed and   $8"$   CMOS Wafer Fabrication  Line is geared-up for production activities.  Three production lots have been processed  with ASICs/IPs/Test Chips designed in-house.  In these lots, 28 designs have been fabricated  and tested successfully. These chips include  some complex ASICs, one of them being  Vikram Processor for Launch Vehicles. SCL

conversation.content: Actually, the idea that mobile ad spend in Eastern Europe is purely chasing tech trends ignores how local consumer behavior and regulatory shifts are reshaping budgets—like how Poland’s strict data laws are forcing brands to pivot from programmatic to contextual ads, not because it’s “trendy,” but because it’s legally necessary. And let’s be real: calling a market “emerging” doesn’t mean it’s naive—it means advertisers who assume one-size-fits-all creative or targeting will get burned by cultural nuance, like Romanian users rejecting overly polished U.S.-style CTAs in favor of community-driven messaging. High-growth doesn’t always mean high-return; some markets like Ukraine are seeing explosive app installs but low retention, making CACs unsustainable unless you adapt content to local pain points, not just algorithms. If your strategy relies on Western benchmarks or global DSPs without localizing creatives or compliance, you’re not innovating—you’re outsourcing risk. True regional success isn’t about spending more—it’s about spending smarter, with teams on the ground who understand that trust is built through relevance, not reach. And if your metrics show rising impressions but flat conversions, maybe the problem isn’t the platform—it’s the assumption that Eastern Europe is just another frontier for scalable automation.

What happens when global DSPs and Western benchmarks fail to account for cultural nuance—does that turn “smart spending” into outsourced risk?  
Is trust in these markets built through reach or relevance—and how do you measure that when impressions rise but conversions flatline?  
And if compliance isn’t just a checkbox but a driver of strategy—as in Poland—should we stop calling these markets “emerging” and start treating them as uniquely governed ecosystems?  
Finally, how do you balance algorithmic efficiency with human insight when the most effective creatives aren’t optimized by AI—but shaped by street-level understanding of local pain points?

Coca-Cola’s “Share a Coke” kept the red script and contour bottle sacred while turning names into emotional currency, proving personalization doesn’t break tradition—it deepens it. Patagonia’s “Don’t Buy This Jacket” campaign honored its outdoor roots by flipping consumerism on its head, showing that legacy isn’t about clinging to old products but defending core values. Even LEGO revived itself not by abandoning bricks, but by embracing digital play through Minecraft collabs and AR apps—tradition as a launchpad, not a cage. These brands didn’t choose between innovation and heritage—they fused them, letting legacy guide the change, not block it. That’s how you stay relevant without erasing who you are.

conversation.content: Aviation’s emissions penalties aren’t driving real change if they’re just absorbed as a cost or passed to passengers—true impact requires forcing operational overhauls, not compliance theater. Airlines treating sustainability as a checkbox risk long-term erosion, while those turning regulations into profit levers through innovation gain competitive edge. The problem isn’t the fines themselves—it’s that thresholds often lag behind tech and fuel advancements, making penalties feel outdated and easily gamed. Real progress demands aligning financial consequences with measurable efficiency gains, like fleet modernization or route optimization, not just hitting arbitrary CO2 targets. If regulators keep setting benchmarks based on legacy models, they’ll miss the chance to incentivize real transformation. Brands winning here aren’t the ones minimizing fines—they’re the ones reengineering operations to make sustainability core to their P&L. And if your ESG report looks clean but your fuel strategy hasn’t evolved, you’re not leading—you’re just rearranging deck chairs. True regulatory alignment means tying every dollar spent on compliance to actual emissions reduction—not just avoiding penalties.
conversation.subtopic: Sustainability and regulatory compliance in aviation, particularly around emissions thresholds and financial penalties.

conversation.content: Airlines like Delta and United are already turning emissions penalties into profit levers by retrofitting older fleets with fuel-efficient engines—cutting CO2 by 15% while avoiding $2M+ in annual fines. Meanwhile, Ryanair’s aggressive route optimization slashed per-passenger emissions by 20%, proving that regulatory pressure can drive efficiency gains if tied to operational KPIs, not just compliance reports. The real failure? Carriers like Lufthansa still treat EU ETS fines as a line-item cost rather than a signal to innovate—resulting in higher ticket prices without actual emissions reductions. When regulators set thresholds based on 2010-era models, airlines game the system by shifting flights to less-regulated regions instead of investing in sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). True progress requires penalties that scale with actual emissions intensity—not arbitrary caps—and reward carriers who adopt SAF or hydrogen tech early. If your sustainability report looks clean but your fleet hasn’t touched SAF since 2022, you’re not compliant—you’re just buying time.
